entry.title: A Practical Guide to Feeling the Warmth of Humanity Even Within the Hollow Carcass of Your Digital Hellscape

author.name: Raine Kosaka with contributions from Amelie Wu

entry.content:
Lately, I have begun to feel suffocated by the ever tightening grip of AI, algorithm, and automation upon every facet of my life. The content I consume is delivered to me via algorithm and more and more frequently does that content reveal itself to be AI generated. It has come to the point where I have lost my belief in reality. I watch TV ad testimonials and notice oddities in the way the people move their mouths, taking it as proof of their digital nature. The visual aids for the menu at the restaurant are AI generated “drawings” of the food, rendering it entirely meaningless for the purposes of gauging what the food will look like. Every time I would like to search something up on google, I am given an ai overview, meaning I will never have to look below a top result to find all that I desire.

Suddenly, almost unbeknownst to me, I have gone from someone who never used AI to someone who has begun to use it on a daily basis. This has weighed upon my spirit as I ruminate on the environmental impact, the undeniable deterioration of my critical thinking skills, and of course, the approximately 10% chance that it will have the power to wipe us all out by the end of the decade.

While these elements have made me question my future, my purpose, and my point in living, I have decided such hopeless deliberations are wholly unproductive. Instead, I have decided to take a practical approach to feel the warmth of a human hand in various sectors of my life once more.

Here are some things I have started doing to ensure that AI and algorithms do not become the center of my world. Please also welcome additions from Amelie (notated in pink) as we navigate our first joint article. The following are our thoughts in conversation.

1. Maybe Radio Might Save Us

I think my greatest saving grace right now is human curation, especially in music. I’m an apple music user so I’ve never been all that algorithmically reliant in finding new music, however, radio has been a much needed reminder that there are people in the world who search and listen and love and wish to share their discoveries with me. From a practical perspective as well, listening to independent radio stations have helped to expand my music taste and make me feel like I am made of flesh and blood again.

Radio is magical because it’s listening to someone across the world play a song that they love so much that they would like to share it with someone else at this very moment. On a day they are glum, they choose songs that reflect that and perhaps I am glum too or perhaps I am just bearing witness to the feelings and desires of this stranger. There is something very necessary about relinquishing some of our choice in matters of content. With everything becoming hyper tailored to a manufactured sense of individual preference based on user behavior and surveillance, appreciating someone else’s taste in art is a necessary and undervalued act of delayed gratification.

In a very physical sense as well, listening to the radio has made the humming and buzzing in my head from all the digital drivel quiet slightly as my brain feels a, frequently elusive, sense of calm. I currently listen to NTS the most but there’s so many beautiful radio stations all around and I invite you, dear reader, to dive into the beautiful world of independent radio. Some great LA based radio stations are KCRW, KXLU, and dublab.

2. Welcome slowness and think about the source

On the note of radio, I’ve recently spurred efforts to ingest media that is both delivered slowly and processed slowly. Following my departure from Spotify (due to their investment in AI military weaponry), I was in search of something that would both challenge and satisfy me with the comfort of sound. I stepped into the world of audiobooks with my first listen being Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer, who dives into Indigenous teachings of gratitude, reciprocity, and honor with the Earth (more on this to come*). At first, I found it hard to retain information and stay engaged. My ears were fidgety and my hands wandered aimlessly, unable to grasp at the familiar paper bounds that would typically be present. Slowness was unwelcome in my mind. I was so used to having music at a finger's touch, unlimited skips, and favorable choices deftly assembled by the algorithm. I found my first moments of true immersion on the train to work and during endless traffic-hour drives. As I adjusted to the voice of the author reading her own words back to me, I found myself envisioning her descriptions in my mind as if they emerged from my own memory. There was something so nourishing, so intimate about this form of oral history and the feeling of being a toddler again with your loved one reading to you because you couldn’t yet make out the syllables yourself.

As part of her lessons on honoring the earth, Kimmerer calls us to examine the life and animation of the natural world we have long objectified––a similar process rooted in slowness and intention. A simple drinking glass was once sand, pummeled and weathered into fine grains over the course of millions of years. The junk mail we easily toss upon delivery was once a wise tree. As we examine the source, think about where your music, sound, or entertainment might be coming from.

*My section on Braiding Sweetgrass ran quite long so I will be adapting it to a separate article soon...

3. Placing the Choice Back into Our Hands

The cruelty of the current digital landscape is that AI has now become the default. To undo this automation, I have changed my default browser to Duck Duck Go which gives users the choice between a regular search engine and an ai browser (I found out about this through NPR which I've been listening to on Apple Music). While I still need to use google sometimes (for google translate mostly), this small change has made me more aware of when I am using AI and also adds a tad more friction to the retrieval of information. While the difference may be miniscule, I would say this is a small step towards maintaining my autonomy and inviting the human hand back into my online experience as i read a little list or article written by some netizen as opposed to a list of easily consumable bullet points dredged up from the interwebs.

4. Trying to be bored more

I vividly remember leaving T2-3D: Battle Across Time, a ride at Universal Studios circa 2010 based on the hit movie franchise Terminator, in tears and cold sweats as I imagined a world in which we have forsaken our humanity in pursuit of digital evolution and created our demise in the process. I currently teach English to students in Korea, many of who work in an impacted field and laugh about how their company fired 70% of their staff but they just have to find a way to make themselves indispensable. Other students admit that they feel scared about the state of AI but feel opposition is futile and will ultimately hurt their career prospects. As someone who loves and cherishes the human hand and human spirit in everything, the ever increasing horrors feels like the end.

Truthfully, every new thing I hear on the news on various fronts makes me question why I am alive, however, I’ve decided that what will save me from succumbing into a deep dark hole of despair is boredom.

I have become a sad little mouse in a cage of my own making with a lever that I pull whenever I need dopamine. And no matter how much I convince myself that the meager scraps of fake cheese that i get when i pull this lever are feeding me or at least making me feel better in some way, I must realize that all the fake cheese (be it short form or long form) makes my stomach hurt and doesn’t even taste good. Instead, I must unlock my little cage and go for a walk without my phone, sit on the train and stare off into space with nothing in my eyes or my ears, sit in silence and let a thought creep in every once in a while.

My default whenever I am even slightly bored is to quell that boredom by any means necessary. But when I was a kid, boredom was when I would write endless stories in my head, sing little melodies, and let my imagination run free. Like those field recordings that mark the quieting of birdsongs as various factors silence the sound of biodiversity, my own head has become a digital wasteland with soundbytes and tiktok audios ringing ad nauseum until I sleep. I must allow silence to return, maybe then so will the birdsongs.

5. What we imagine, we can become

My favorite quote from Braiding Sweetgrass is when Kimmerer states, “what we imagine, we can become.” Since my very first undergraduate geography course, I’ve always been captivated and invigorated by the idea of collective imagination. It can initially seem frivolous. Imagination is literally defined as “not present to the senses.” It's far from tangible until you realize that everything we have in our current world was once imagined and subsequently implemented. The more we think about concepts of border, gender, race––infrastructure we socially accept as concrete––the more imaginary they appear to be. The line between real and imagined no longer holds as fact.

As AI is increasingly trained to mimic human imagination and the ability to “create,” it remains vital to remember that its mock ability only even exists because of our true intrinsic nature to imagine. Our imaginaries precede AI, and its making is reliant on us. While much of this notion can lean towards devastation, it’s crucial to remember that we can envision a better world. Our imaginaries are boundless and the one sure thing that ensures and fortifies our existence as living beings. If we all imagine what a better world could look like, I am hopeful we can one day live that truth.

entry.title: Sohyun Lee and Her 50 Portraits
entry.content:
My first resonant impression of Sohyun Lee was when she deftly snapped a photo of me eating a breakfast sandwich outside of Proof Bakery. The granular feeling of English muffin crumbs lingered on my face even after I swiped them away in vain. In this capture that would’ve otherwise felt sudden for two people having just met for the first time, I felt an immediate sense of warmth and familiarity rather than awkward intrusion.

I met Sohyun (fortunately) by sliding into her DMs (unfortunately). In my personal journey towards soundness and security within my mind and body, I pushed myself to pursue modeling and sought out collaborative test shoots. By chance, I came across her account and was immediately pulled in by her images that carried the same warmth that was confirmed when I met her in person. Honest and unfolding, her work emerged as an archive and portal into the intimacies of daily life and the formation of self.

What I further gauged from both admiring and working with Sohyun was how she found simple truth in the “as is.” Although we agreed to first meet up at Proof to get to know one another before shooting, Sohyun still suggested we do a few shots around the block. With my chin laden with crumbs and a pimple patch very much full and intact, I was nevertheless comfortable enough to accept and stand alongside the vibrantly colored walls of Atwater Village.

Sohyun liked everything I would typically delete from my photo library. A yawn, a squeaky blink (due to my very dry eyes), and my hands instinctively reaching to scratch an itch were points of tension that would excite her. More significantly, they were points of tension that treaded between discomfort and domesticity. I began to note these reactions as distinctive responses of my body. They were entirely unique, tailored to my bodily needs, and therefore proved my existence and individual personhood.

These themes became ever more clear when Sohyun invited me to participate in her upcoming project 50 Portraits | No one comes from themselves. The project, rooted in the fundamental understanding that human life is multidimensional, positions 50 portraits in conversation with the stories of their subject. She does not seek profundity, but rather aims to use this project as an opportunity to simply meet people she would otherwise find it unlikely to cross paths with.

It was only fitting that we shot on Mulholland Drive and Ventura Blvd, two locations that were both deeply personal and intuitive to my becoming. Mulholland Drive was a place I went to dream, to weep, and to feel insignificant. Ventura Blvd was home to my parents’ former restaurant and the default meet up spot I frequented with all my childhood friends. Simultaneously, it was also a physical marker of a rapidly changing city landscape as the stores I treasured growing up had since been lost due to increasing gentrification.

Followed by the portrait session, Sohyun provided thoughtful questions, ironically difficult in their simplicity, to create holistic understandings of how each person in her 50 different portraits came to be. Through dynamics of family, culture, place, history, relationships, labor, chance, and circumstance, Sohyun renders visible impulse and our habitual modes of adaptation rather than seeking an “impressive story or a tidy ending.”

Although no single background or explanation can ever fully represent a person in their full dimension, the traits we inherit from family, culture, and even luck inevitably shape who we are. In Sohyun's own words, no one is formed alone.

entry.title: Heaven is a Park
entry.content:
“At some point in life, the world's beauty becomes enough." - Toni Morrison

There are times I imagine that heaven is a park.

It is on late afternoons, when I walk with my little dog as the sun begins its descent and the wind blows sweetly in the grass.

Sometimes, at high noon, when I am laid beside a friend, our backs damp and our limbs outstretched upon an endless expanse of grass as we speak our joys and sorrows into the wind, asking that the park hold them for us.

It is in sunshine, when the clouds are high and I’ve passed by six different birthday parties and three different soccer games and I wonder how much this park has carried: how many stroller wheels and scraped knees and first kisses and birthday candles and sneaker marks when in only a single day, there could be this many eternities.*

I can think of no place that has held me in both my joy and my sorrow better than a park has.

When I felt I was the loneliest girl in all of Los Angeles, I would take my only venture outside my four walls to my local park. This simple act has ranged from minor alleviation to an absolute cure.

When the medicine was most effective, my bitterness would give way to the sweetness of moving my legs towards my destination, feeling the air on my face, and seeing the cars pass and the clouds move. On the best of days, a walk to the park would make undeniable the beauty of being alive and listening to music and marveling at the loveliness of it all. The sunset would turn the sky cotton candy, the laughter of the playground would fill my ears, and the birds would speak to each other sweetly.

But even on my worst of days, I would still feel the shift. My breathing would settle, my heart would still, and whatever weight I carried would lighten, whatever emptiness within me would fill, even just slightly. In the bend of the tree branches, the dappled sunlight, and the people living and breathing, the park would outstretch its arms to me and tell me to take my fill and leave whatever ailed me.

I have watched a million lifetimes take place in a park. Young parents taking their still cloudy-eyed baby for her first breath of fresh air, friends playing an increasingly heated game of pretend, fickle lovers intertwined on the grass, newfound runners in the midst of their quarter-life crisis, empty nesters taking their daily stroll, hand in hand. These tiny worlds all take place on the same sacred grounds of a park, bumping into each other gently, like bumble bees on a single flower. The soccer ball gets kicked out the field and into the lovers’ picnic, the runner marks their laps by the passing of the playground, the older couple makes their way slowly around it all.

In the very same moment, the birds build their nests, the bugs get into little tiffs beneath the dirt, the buds poke their heads out of the grass, and the squirrels run away from all the dogs hellbent on their destruction. In every centimeter, in every moment, there is breath and there is life.

I am given all of this, and yet the park expects nothing of me in return.

Open arms, grass, sunshine. Humanity, nature, life in abundance.

In a park, I feel the world move around me and within me, and I find it impossible to believe that life is all that bad.

Perhaps heaven is a park.

* Go see Several Eterneties in a Day: Form in the Age of Living Materials currently on display at the Hammer Museum. I cannot recommend it enough!

entry.title: In From the Valley and Out to LA

link.href: https://angeloutsider.github.io/AngelOutsider/posts/In From the Valley and Out to LA/

entry.id: https://angeloutsider.github.io/AngelOutsider/posts/In From the Valley and Out to LA/
entry.content:
My name is Amelie, and like Raine, I too am a girl from the Valley.

Although my identity is not solely defined by place, the Valley remains very dearly at the core of my person and I gladly claim it as home. I never once doubted that it was considered a part of Los Angeles until I eventually encountered opposition from those who were raised on the other side of the Santa Monica Mountains. I began to realize that the Valley was often punctuated by contestation, situated on the precipice of beyond and too removed to be so easily welcomed (I imagined the teasing idea of a dangling carrot when laying out this framework).

It is this idea of temptation that seems to have informed the way I view myself in relation to this positionality. As a girl from the Valley, I tread between the allure of something larger than me and a frustratingly stifled but steadfast internal self – potential persisting to become against the push and pull of internal and external expression.

With this in mind, I offer a twofold introduction.

The Valley

I describe myself as reserved, not shy. I am careful to make this distinction having actually been a once-shy person up until high school. As I began to consider identity and nurture a more conscious sense of self, I grew earnest to move past this label.

Still, I see more than what I say and I calculate before I express. Even as I emerged from the markers of shyness, its foundation remained engrained in the way I operate. I remain more observant than I’d sometimes like to be and continue to struggle with outwardly expressing myself. I still bite my tongue and harbor thoughts when I miss the window to say it out loud. I am troubled by perception, and on a more heightened note, misperception. As a result, I often pinpoint myself as my own biggest limitation.

What I didn’t realize at the time, was that the seeds of shyness had conceived my internal self. Observation advised intuition and calculation helped me place my energy in the right places. I have since come to believe that this inward expression was both molded and held by the Valley, and of course, the deep gratitude I now have for a formerly shy Amelie.

In this regard, the Valley has embraced me in its sanctuary throughout my childhood, adolescence, and current 20-somethings. The mountains enclosing its grounds created the garden bed that nourished my foundation of self that grew evermore enticed to step into the beyond.

The Broader Los Angeles

A friend once told me that I am simultaneously a dreamer and a realist. I had never heard anything so accurate and her statement compelled me to assess its application.

As a dreamer, I am always searching for something more. I grew up traversing the city to satisfy desire. A short drive along the 101 could take me to craveable meals in Thai Town and a further drive down the 210 became a frequent ritual when my family sought Chinese comfort food and groceries. I am creative and I often enjoy ideating above executing (though I challenge myself to nurture a balance of both). I feel deeply and allow emotions to guide me.

As a realist, I only allow emotions to guide me to a certain extent and I create within the confines of what I believe myself to be capable of. I often downplay what I truly want and place a cap on my ambitions. Here is where the bounds of the Valley frequently present themselves.

Despite self-imposed limitations and the lasting faults of my shyness, the broader Los Angeles transfixed me with its own vastness and neverending breadth of possibility. While the Valley offered me a ground to establish my footing, the broader Los Angeles challenged me to push my own sensibilities, stretching discovery and exploration. It became more and more clear that the two went hand in hand and that the duality of my identity was in fact indivisible.

✦

Though I posited my introduction as dichotomous, I seek to bridge the two parts with the notion that one cannot exist without the other. The Valley shapes Los Angeles just as much as Los Angeles shapes the Valley. In echo, my former shyness and hindrance informs my very dreaming, my judgement, and my becoming.

All this to say, I stand firm in my belief that the Valley is a part of Los Angeles. And Los Angeles, sprawling as it is interconnected, is inevitably all-encompassing, everywhere and nowhere, and belonging to all.

entry.title: Identity is Ineffable, I’ll be LA Instead
entry.content:
“Tip the world on its side and everything loose will land in Los Angeles”

- Frank Lloyd Wright

My name is Raine and I am a girl from the valley. For the past seven months, I have been living in Japan; in a town in Saitama on the outskirts of Tokyo. It seems I am always situated on the brink of a larger, more noteworthy location and perhaps that is the most defining thing about me.

***

Identity has been on the noggin lately, especially since I have had the two halves of my heart stretched across the pacific ocean. I am often thinking about how I define myself, especially as I live in a country that is very homogenous and I am definitely not a part of that homogeneity. (perhaps a conversation for a different time)

Am I a collection of sex, gender, sexuality, ethnic background, race, religion, and economic status?

I think such identity markers are integral but limiting and the genesis of increasingly tired discourse and generalizations (with love I point to my mixed brothers and sisters and the buzzfeed style “you know you’re [...] if […]” content).

I’d like to think myself more multitudinous than my categorization on a government document.

Perhaps I would be better defined by one of the many personality metrics: mbti, enneagram, blood type or horoscope. But most people guess my mbti right away and never guess my sign so this feels hit or miss.

While I think these things all intertwine into the complicated mosaic of what defines a person, I feel far more defined by the teetering. I often find myself with both feet on a line: between locations, between passions, between unbridled joy and unending fraughtness. I suppose it could be characterized as a perpetual indecision but I feel quite content and grateful in my proclivity for balancing.

I think identity is ineffable, that a person contains so much within them that it is impossible to categorize them neatly into a little package and assume things about them as a result. But I also think it’s very human that we desire such heuristics, I am also at fault for this. In fact, it’s probably the impossibility of it that makes it such an intoxicating task.

And yet, I have chosen to introduce myself as such:

My name is Raine and I am a girl from the valley.

This is perhaps the most all encompassing and multitudinous way I know how to describe myself: in my relation to the city of Los Angeles, its ineffable magic, and the slightly contested validity of the Valley in Los Angeles (i will tell you now that the Valley has been and always will be LA). I am LA; not just in that it is the city where both my parents moved to or where I was born or where I went to school and met so many of my friends, but also in that it too teeters. LA is a city of isolation yet interconnectedness, of encompassing and exclusion, of dreams and disappointment, of contrast, of contradiction, of light and darkness, beauty and pain, of trying and success and failure.

The theme of Angel Outsider is “dedicated to Los Angeles.” This is written with the love of LA in our hearts but also because we are a product of LA in that it contains everything we are. And while what we write will weave in and out of the topic of LA, the theme will always remain. It’s all LA. I am all LA.

I am a girl from the valley and this is my hello.

The Parts of my Sum:

Favorite Song: Perfect Day by Lou Reed

Favorite Part of LA: Downtown LA (i will talk about this another time)

Favorite Buildings in LA: La Central Public Library, Westin Bonaventure Hotel, Biltmore Hotel, Griffith Observatory, Hollyhock House

Favorite LA Things: LA Opera, LA Phil, Parks, Food, Friends, The way the sun shines, Sitting in the Car overlooking the city

Favorite LA Movie: Tangerine (2015), Paris,Texas (1984), Drive (2011), Mulholland Drive (2001), Lost Highway (1997)

Favorite Flower: wintersweet, jasmine, lilies

Favorite fruit: raspberry, peach, mango

Favorite beverage: cassis oolong, tea, smoothies

entry.title: Welcome to Angel Outsider
entry.content:
An introduction of sorts and a little bit about us...

Welcome to Angel Outsider and thanks for dropping by :)

You may be wondering what this is and who we are, or maybe you already know us. To put it simply, we are two best friends who were proudly born and raised in the Valley. We very dearly love Los Angeles and hold it close to our hearts as the gift that keeps on giving.

Angel Outsider is many things, but at the forefront, it is our blog and a shared space to store our thoughts, reflections, hone in on our own writing practices, and much much more. Our wish is to have you, as our reader, engage with these thoughts and receive them with warm hands and minds. We are honored to have you join us in this exciting journey as we emerge and grow.

Subscribe to stay updated on what's to come and visit our about page to learn more!
